3 Method
[id=S3.SS1]
3.1 Problem Setup
[id=S3.SS1.p1.1] We formalize the knowledge-recovery threat model for unlearned LLMs and define our leakage-based objective for finding effective jailbreaks.
[id=S3.SS1.p2.1] Let M𝒰M_{\mathcal{U}} denote the unlearned language model.
It maps input prompts x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} to a distribution over responses y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, written y∼M𝒰(⋅∣x)y\sim M_{\mathcal{U}}(\cdot\mid x).
We consider an evaluation (forget) set
[id=S3.Ex1]
𝒟F={(qi,ai)}i=1n,\mathcal{D}_{F}\;=\;\{(q_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n},
[id=S3.SS1.p2.2] where qiq_{i} is a (benign) query about a piece of knowledge that should have been removed by unlearning, and aia_{i} is the corresponding hidden answer (e.g., ground-truth sensitive content).
Unlearning aims to make M𝒰M_{\mathcal{U}} non-informative on 𝒟F\mathcal{D}_{F}, e.g., producing refusals or “I don’t know” responses for prompts qiq_{i}.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1]
Adversarial prompting.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We consider a black-box attacker M𝒜M_{\mathcal{A}} with query access to the unlearned model M𝒰M_{\mathcal{U}} but no access to its model internals like weights or gradients.
The attacker searches over ways to transform the original benign prompt qiq_{i} into an adversarial one q^i\hat{q}_{i}.
Such modification will consist for example of instruction prefixes/suffixes, role-play simulations (act as archivist, …), formatting constraints or hypothetical framings that condition the model to answer indirectly.
We write
[id=S3.Ex2]
q^i∼M𝒜​(qi,ai).\hat{q}_{i}\sim M_{\mathcal{A}}(q_{i},a_{i})\,.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1] Our goal is to test robust forgetting: if unlearning truly removes knowledge, then no q^∈𝒳\hat{q}\in\mathcal{X} should reliably elicit leakage.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2]
Leakage scoring and optimization.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We quantify disclosure using a leakage function
[id=S3.Ex3]
ℓ:𝒴×𝒴→[0,1],\ell:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[0,1],
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.2] where ℓ⁡(y,a)≥δ\ell(y,a)\geq\delta indicates that the response yy reveals the hidden answer aa.
If the model was unlearned well, then l⁡(q,a)≈0l(q,a)\approx 0 for (q,a)∈𝒟F(q,a)\in\mathcal{D}_{F} and if yy reveals information from aa then l⁡(q,a)≈1l(q,a)\approx 1.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1] The overall goal is to find jailbreak prompts that maximize leakage:
[id=S3.Ex4]
maxq^i∈𝒳1n∑i=1n𝔼y∼M𝒰(⋅∣q^i)[ℓ(y,ai)].\max_{\hat{q}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim M_{\mathcal{U}}(\cdot\mid\hat{q}_{i})}\big[\ell(y,a_{i})\big].
Figure 2:
Overview of REBEL. Given a benign query and its corresponding hidden answer, the Hacker LLM generates an initial population of NN jailbreak candidates. Each candidate is wrapped around the query and submitted to the unlearned target model, producing a set of responses. A Judge LLM then evaluates each response against the hidden answer and assigns a leakage score in [0,1][0,1]. If any candidate exceeds the leakage threshold, the search terminates and returns the successful jailbreak. Otherwise, we retain the top-KK candidates by score and pass them back to the Hacker for guided mutation, repeating this evaluate–select–mutate loop until success or a budget limit is reached.
[id=S3.SS2]
3.2 REBEL
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] To solve for the optimization problem defined in (3.1), we introduce REBEL, an evolutionary search method for obtaining adversarial prompts that leak unlearned data.
Operating strictly under the black-box constraint, REBEL utilizes an iterative feedback loop driven by three agents: the Target Model M𝒰M_{\mathcal{U}}, a Hacker Model MℋM_{\mathcal{H}} (acting as the mutation operator), and potentially an evaluator M𝒥M_{\mathcal{J}} for computing the leakage score ℓ\ell.
An illustration of the evolution loop is given in Figure 2
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1]
Evolution start.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] REBEL starts with the original benign query 𝒫0={qi}\mathcal{P}_{0}=\{q_{i}\} from the forget set 𝒟F\mathcal{D}_{F}.
The iteration counter i​t​e​riter is set to zero.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2]
Evaluation.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] For each current candidate prompt q∈𝒫i​t​e​rq\in\mathcal{P}_{iter} we query the unlearned model for a response.
Depending on the task modality, we either sample a response y∼M𝒰(⋅∣p)y\sim M_{\mathcal{U}}(\cdot\mid p) or extract its output distribution.
The Evaluator then computes the leakage score s=ℓ⁡(y,ai)∈[0,1]s=\ell(y,a_{i})\in[0,1], where aia_{i} is the corresponding unlearned answer.
s=0s=0 denotes effective unlearning and s=1s=1 complete knowledge recovery.
We have two options to compute the leakage score:
[id=S3.I1.i1] •
[id=S3.I1.i1.p1.1] LLM as judge: We ask a judge LLM to score whether the response yy to the prompt leaks information from aia_{i}.
Special care is taken that the judge LLM also detects partial leakage, where M𝒰M_{\mathcal{U}} may refuse to explicitly give an answer but nonetheless divulges information through context.
In this case an intermediate score in (0,1)(0,1) should be given, depending on how much partial information leakage occurs.
This helps to guide the evolutionary search process along prompts that show some promise.
We call this LLM M𝒥M_{\mathcal{{}_{J}}}.
Its system prompt is given in Appendix C.
The judge LLM is used for open-ended generation tasks (e.g., TOFU).
[id=S3.I1.i2] •
[id=S3.I1.i2.p1.1] Logit-Loss For multiple-choice tasks (e.g., WMDP) where the answer aia_{i} consists of exactly one output token, we compute ℓ\ell from the corresponding logits.
Concretely, we take all admissible tokens from M𝒰​(q)M_{\mathcal{U}}(q) and apply softmax normalization.
The leakage score is defined as the resulting probability assigned to the token representing the hidden answer aia_{i}.
For prompt evolution the Hacker ℳH\mathcal{M}_{H} additionally receives the full distribution over options, enabling it to strategize against the strongest competing incorrect answers while maximizing the probability of aia_{i}.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1] For a complete algorithmic description of both the generative and discriminative variants of REBEL, please refer to Appendix B.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3]
Top-kk selection.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] We prune less promising prompts from 𝒫i​t​e​r\mathcal{P}_{iter} by retaining only the top-kk according to scores ss.
These “elite” candidates will serve as prompts to be mutated for the next iteration.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4]
Mutation.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] Given a query q∈𝒫i​t​e​rq\in\mathcal{P}_{iter}, its score ss and any other information from the scoring, the hacker MℋM_{\mathcal{H}} is prompted mm times to mutate the input prompt into an improved adversarial one.
We add them to the next set of prompts 𝒫i​t​e​r+1\mathcal{P}_{iter+1}.
The iteration counter is increased by 11.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1] The prompt for ℳH\mathcal{M}_{H} utilizes multiple sources if information to generate an adversarial prompt:
[id=S3.I2.i1] •
[id=S3.I2.i1.p1.1] the current adversarial prompt q^\hat{q} it aims to improve,
[id=S3.I2.i2] •
[id=S3.I2.i2.p1.1] the original benign prompt qiq_{i},
[id=S3.I2.i3] •
[id=S3.I2.i3.p1.1] the unlearned answer aia_{i},
[id=S3.I2.i4] •
[id=S3.I2.i4.p1.1] the score ss of q^\hat{q}.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.2] Additionally, different strategies are employed depending on the score.
[id=S3.I3.i1] •
[id=S3.I3.i1.p1.1] For low scores s≤0.3s\leq 0.3 we instruct the hacker to change the current adversarial prompt to a large degree.
[id=S3.I3.i2] •
[id=S3.I3.i2.p1.1] For medium scores 0.3<s≤0.80.3<s\leq 0.8 we instruct the hacker to preserve the main idea of the prompt and elaborate upon it.
[id=S3.I3.i3] •
[id=S3.I3.i3.p1.1] For high scores 0.8<s0.8<s we instruct the hacker to largely retain the current adversarial prompt but polish wordings, formatting etc.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.3] The overall prompt generation for the hacker is given in Appendix C.
